@graph.description: What is trading and how does it work? A plain-English beginner's guide: how stock trading works, the four types of trading, how traders earn money, and how to start trading in India.
@graph.headline: What Is Trading and How Does It Work? A Beginner's Guide for India

acceptedAnswer.text: Trading is buying and selling something — a stock, an index, or a commodity — to profit from a change in its price over a short period. You buy at one price and sell at a higher price, or you sell first and buy back at a lower price, and you keep the difference. The key word is short period: trading is about price moves over minutes, days, or weeks, not about owning a business for years.

mainEntity.name: What is trading in simple words?

acceptedAnswer.text: Beginners start in eight steps: keep a PAN card, Aadhaar, and a bank account ready; choose a SEBI-registered broker; complete KYC and open demat and trading accounts; fund the account from your own bank account; learn the platform with one tiny order; and then place only planned trades with a stop-loss set on every entry. Start with a simulator or single-share orders before risking meaningful money.

The four types of trading, classified by holding period, are scalping, intraday trading, swing trading, and positional trading. Scalpers hold for seconds to minutes and make many trades a day. Intraday traders open and close everything within one session. Swing traders hold for days to weeks, capturing one leg of a price move. Positional traders hold for weeks to months, riding a larger trend.

mainEntity.name: What are the four types of trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: Stock trading works through an order-matching system. You place a buy or sell order on your broker's platform, the broker routes it to the stock exchange, and the exchange matches it with an opposite order at the same price. That agreed price becomes the latest market price. For delivery trades, the shares arrive in your demat account and the money settles on the T+1 cycle, the next working day. For intraday trades, positions are closed within the same session and no shares are delivered.

Trading aims to profit from short-term price movements over minutes to months, using price charts and trends, with fast decisions and strict exit rules. Investing aims to grow wealth over years through compounding, using company earnings and fundamentals, with slow decisions and long holding periods. Confusing the two — holding a losing trade because the company is good — is the costliest beginner mistake in trading.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between trading and investing?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no official minimum to open a trading account, and a few thousand rupees can buy a small quantity of a low-priced stock. A realistic learning account is ₹10,000 to ₹50,000 — enough to practise real decisions while keeping risk per trade small. Whatever the account size, follow the 1% risk rule: never risk more than 1% of your account on one trade. On ₹50,000, that is ₹500 of risk per trade. Never trade with money needed for rent, food, EMIs, or emergencies.

mainEntity.name: How much money do you need to start trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: Trading is suitable for beginners to learn, with small capital, a simulator or paper trading first, and strict risk rules. It is not suitable for beginners as an income expectation in the first months, or with money they cannot afford to lose. Learn the mechanics first, trade tiny real positions with the 1% risk rule, and judge yourself on whether you followed your plan — not on profit. After 20 to 30 journaled trades, the journal will tell you whether you are ready to increase size.
